title: From efficient nitrite accumulation to complete collapse: how a microbial community and its antibiotic resistance genes in a nitrification system respond to long-term exposure to ciprofloxacin and copper
description: Heavy metals and antibiotics converge in wastewater treatment systems, presenting a co-stress whose long-term ecological impacts remains unclear. In this study, 1, 10 and 30 mg/L ciprofloxacin (CIP) and 3 mg/L copper (Cu) were selected as representative pollutants in a sequencing batch reactor (SBR) that was operated for 240 days. The long-term effects of this co-stress was investigated for nitrification performance, microbial community structure and composition, abundance of functional bacteria, archaea and their functional genes, and antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs). The co-stress of 1 mg/L CIP and 3 mg/L Cu hampered nitrification in the activated sludge system, and this inhibition remained at 10 mg/L CIP with 3 mg/L Cu. Although the ammonia nitrogen removal rate efficiency (ANRE) was restored to 100% over time, the nitrite accumulation rate was raised to 80%. When the CIP concentration was increased to 30 mg/L, the ANRE dropped to 37% and sludge bulking occurred. After pollutant withdrawal, instead of recovering, the ANRE further fell to below 10%. Although the applied co-stress changed the relative abundance of core genera, conditionally rare taxa (CRT) consistently remained the main core groups. Co-stress eventually reduced the relative abundances of conventional nitrifying bacteria AOB (e.g., Nitrosomonas) and NOB (e.g., Nitrospira), as well as their functional genes (e.g., amoA/B and hao). Meanwhile, enzymes controlling ammonia-L-glutamate interconversion (e.g., glutamine synthetase, glutamate synthase, glutamate dehydrogenase) were highly abundant. In total, 68 ARG subtypes were detected. Multidrug-resistant and beta-lactam ARGs were significantly enriched and dominated efflux and inactivation mechanisms, thereby inducing and enhancing microbial resistance. Nitrogen-fixing genera were identified as important potential hosts of ARGs (e.g., NorBC, mdtO and spcN). Complex co-occurrence relationships existed between nitrogen metabolism functional genes and ARGs. During sludge bulking, the relative abundance of filamentous bacteria (in particular Flavobacterium and to some extent Acidovorax) increased significantly. Overall, co-stress disrupted the microbial community structure, particularly suppressing nitrifying bacteria and their functional genes, thereby leading to nitrite accumulation. Prolonged high-intensity stress further caused system performance collapse and induced sludge bulking, a process that may in turn promote the dissemination of ARGs.
